p: And just one final question, I mean, yeah, question about dog poop. How much funds are being allocated to the dog waste dispenser pilot?

I would like to expand that to my District, just put it out there. Before we get started with Council Member Ung, given that we were talking about equipment and capital budget priorities, I just want to ask a few quick questions about that.

COMMITTEE ON SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 92 We have 1.13 billion allocated for equipment replacement over five years. What percentage of this is dedicated to replacing the aging collection truck fleet versus transitioning to mechanical trucks for containerization?

Okay. So, as far as equipment funds allocated for equipment replacements, we have 1.13 billion allocated for equipment replacement over every vehicle type. So, the highest amount that we have is the reloading collection trucks, which is an eight-year life cycle along with dual-bin collections, it's an eight-year life cycle. And then our (INAUDIBLE) which is a smaller equipment, is an eight-year life cycle. So, those are the trucks that we make sure that we're replenishing them appropriately. And as far as the containerization initiatives right now, all of our new rear-loading

COMMITTEE ON SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 93 collection trucks and dual bin trucks are being outfitted with tippers. And then we're internally working on coming up with cost estimates as far as the expansion of the entry containerization initiative.

So, the Bronx garage replacement project. Curious if there are any cost overruns or delays affecting this project. And how does this impact the Department's ability to maintain adequate garage capacity citywide?

So right now, we do not anticipate any cost overruns, but that'll likely be evaluated at the conclusion of construction. We're estimated to start construction at the start of 2027 with the completion date of 2034.
What is the current 10-year capital plan for DSNY, and how is the 3.54 billion allocated between equipment and garages?

So, our 10-year capital commitment plan, which spans from FY 2026 to FY 2035 is about 3.26 billion. And out of that, approximately 63 percent is allocated to

COMMITTEE ON SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 94 equipment and then 33 percent is allocated to facilities, which is about 1.1 billion dollars.

So, the main two front line collection vehicle vehicles, heavy duty vehicles are our rear-loading collection trucks and our dual bin collection trucks. So, for FY27, we anticipate replacing 104 of the rear-loading collection trucks, which have a price tag of about 545,000 dollars. And then our dual bin collection trucks for FY27, we anticipate replacing 80 of those, and the price tag on those about 573,000 dollars.
Beyond the Bronx garage, are there any capital projects experiencing any significant delays or cost overruns? And if so, what steps are being taken to bring them back on track?

As of currently, we are not anticipating any significant delays and no cost overruns in any of the projects you mentioned.

COMMITTEE ON SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 95
Great. And then what percentage of the capital budget is allocated to sustainability initiatives such as electric or hybrid vehicle purchases or charging infrastructure?
I have to get back to you on that, Chair.
Thank you. How does the Department prioritize capital investments across competing needs like fleet replacement, garage upgrades, containerization, infrastructure, transportation?

Sure. So obviously, you know, vehicle replacement is one of the things that we always want to make sure that we're not falling behind on because then there is a cascading effect. Unfortunately, we saw some of that during COVID where we didn't purchase any heavy duty vehicles, and then that created a ripple effect with, you know, we had to shift some of the operations to subsequent shifts, and, you know, then there's extra overtime added to repair some of these aging vehicles. So, that's the priority. And then as far as capital investments for our facilities, that's one of

COMMITTEE ON SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 96 the things that, you know, we always want to make sure that we're investing in our facilities, but I think there's a delicate balance. As I mentioned, 66 percent of that goes to the fleet, and the remaining goes to our facilities. Oh, and then just going back, I have the number. So, as far as electric vehicles, as far as sustainability initiatives, we have 25 small alley collection trucks and then we are replacing. It's about 360 million for bike lane equipment, which is a battery electric vehicle, which is a small sweepers that we have.
Thank you. What is the expected useful life of new collection trucks being procured, and how does this compare to the current fleet age?

So, the rear-loading and dual bin collection trucks useful life is about eight years, and right now the average is about five years for rear-loading collection trucks and about five and a half years for dual bin trucks.

Are there opportunities to extend the useful life of existing

COMMITTEE ON SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 97 equipment through enhanced maintenance programs, thereby reducing capital replacement costs?

Sure. And that's one of the things that we always look for. We work with DCAS on that, and we're always exploring strategies on new best practices, you know, maintenance approaches, things like that. But, yeah, that's one of the things that we always look for to expand that.
Curious, how much has been allocated for marine transfer station upgrades and maintenance in the current capital plan?
So, there's about 38 million dollars allocated to 10-year capital commitment plan for marine transfer station upgrades and maintenance.
And could you elaborate a little bit on the role the capital budget plays in supporting the transition to mechanical collection for containerization?

Sure. So, that's one of the things that we are evaluating. We put out an RFP for the side loading collection truck and that was thankfully approved. Now we are working

COMMITTEE ON SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 98 to see what the expansion of a potential citywide rollout would be. And I think that's one of those things that once we nail down a number, we'll be able to then have a better sense of what that commitment would be on the capital plan.
Thank you. And I am so sorry, but I completely overlooked Council Member Brewer and I want to make sure.
Thank you very much and thank you for your testimony, which is very detailed and like everybody else, Frank Lettera is a rock star. But so is Glennn Baldwin, who is the District Manager in 7.
Good to hear.

Sure. So, 3-1-1…

Yep. I don't think the public doesn't understand. I think they

Just one final question. So, there aren't a lot of tow locations, nothing in Manhattan. But the tow companies, you said you had four contracts. They take it to their own

COMMITTEE ON SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 106 place. They don't take it to a PD or one of your tow places.

Do you have any sense of some of them? You don't have plates on them. But if they do have plates, you have some sense it's ghost plates or you just don't know. You don't keep track of that.

Thank you, Council Member Brewer. Really quick before we continue. I want to make sure that we're touching quickly on waste export costs. What is the Department's current annual expenditure on waste export, and how does the

COMMITTEE ON SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 107 budgeted nearly 600 million compare to actual spending? And how has this figure evolved in the past five fiscal years?

So the 594.8 million dollars, generally we think that does reflect what we expect to spend this year. You know, adjustments are made each year in our budget to reflect actual tonnage on the street. I think the hard thing here is you have two main components that contribute to the cost. You have what the actual tonnage is that we collected, which is an uncontrollable. And then we do have long-term waste export contracts. And the pricing is very predictable. Each year we get an increase based on the consumer price index so we have that all contracted out and under control.
Are there any additional factors that contribute to the increase in waste export costs beyond inflation and the adjustments?
It's the adjustments and then it's what tonnage we collected.

How do the terms of the Department's long-term waste export

COMMITTEE ON SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 108 contracts impact current and future budget projections?

Yeah. I mean, you know, we don't always know what the CPI is going to be going into future years, but it's generally predictable and it's within a range so that's really how we project into the future, at least in terms of contractual rates.
Are there opportunities to renegotiate existing waste export contracts to achieve more favorable terms?

So, we put together these long-term contracts with the idea of not having fluctuations and volatility in the market. So, our main contractors we have set for the for the long term so we really don't have any opportunities to renegotiate any sort of major terms in those contracts in the near future.
What, if any, operational efficiencies have you implemented or planned to implement to help reduce the per ton cost of waste export?

So, one of the things that we have worked with the vendors is to

COMMITTEE ON SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 109 make sure we have the staffing of the transfer stations right-sized and appropriate. You know, when these transfer stations were first put into place, there was an idea of what would be appropriate, and then obviously, over time, since we've had the transfer stations open for some time now, we've been able to make staffing adjustments within that, and that's been able to control our cost per ton.

While there has been a small reduction, it's been an increase, nonetheless, from 17 percent to 19.4 percent in terms of our recycling diversion rate. How have any waste reduction initiatives such as citywide curb composting affected the volume of waste requiring export and associated costs?
I mean, I think as a general matter, the cost per ton on organic waste and on exporting refuse are roughly the same so it's really just a transferring it from one place to another.

And finally, what alternative waste management strategies is the Department exploring to mitigate rising export costs, and what are some potential projected savings?

COMMITTEE ON SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 110

I can take that, Chair. So, I think one of the things that we think would be very effective is EPR. I think EPR, and I know there's that State legislation that it's in discussion now. I think that's where we would see the biggest shift as far as kind of any kind of savings for export costs and obviously diversion rates and things like that. So, EPR is one of the things that we support and I think would be beneficial to that.
